Chapter Seven: The Anointing—Healing, Belonging, and Joy.
There’s this quiet ritual that often slips right past anyone who’s not paying close attention—a shepherd anointing his sheep with oil. It might seem like a simple gesture, but honestly, it’s packed with meaning. Back in ancient times, people used oil for all sorts of reasons: to heal cuts and scrapes, to soothe irritation, even to keep pests away. For the sheep, that gentle touch of oil was the shepherd’s way of saying, “I see you. I care.” It was a moment of healing and real relief.
Picture this: it’s a warm summer evening, and the air is buzzing with insects. The sheep are restless—shaking their heads, stomping their feet, clearly uncomfortable. But then, the shepherd makes his way through the flock, carrying a small flask of oil. With steady, gentle hands, he rubs it on their heads and noses, soothing the irritation and keeping those pesky flies away. Almost immediately, you can see the sheep relax. Their discomfort melts away, just because the shepherd noticed and cared enough to help.
You know, life can feel a lot like that sometimes. We all go through stretches where little irritations pile up or we carry wounds no one else can see. Maybe it’s a disappointment, a heartbreak, or just the grind of daily struggles. The shepherd’s anointing is this beautiful reminder: your hurts matter. Healing isn’t just possible—it’s offered, even in the messy middle of everyday life. That oil isn’t just a remedy. It’s a mark of belonging, a quiet way of saying, “You’re mine. I see your pain, and I care.”
Imagine one of the sheep comes back to the flock with a scratch on its ear—a souvenir from a thorny bramble on the hillside. The shepherd doesn’t just ignore it. He kneels down, cleans the wound, and gently applies oil. The sheep might flinch at first, but pretty soon, it relaxes. Healing starts with that small, caring act.
Most of us carry wounds that don’t show—things like betrayal, loss, or disappointment that we tuck away where no one else looks. But the shepherd’s anointing shows us another way to live. It says, “Yes, pain is real, but it doesn’t get the final word.” Healing comes not just from what’s applied, but from the relationship itself—the comfort of knowing someone is really paying attention, that every hurt matters.
There’s another layer here, too—belonging. Through this simple ritual, the sheep are marked as part of the flock, set apart by the shepherd’s care. That touch of oil isn’t just about healing; it’s about identity. It’s the assurance that they’re not alone. And let’s be honest, that desire to belong, to know you’re part of something, runs deep in all of us. The shepherd’s touch answers both needs: a safe place in the flock, and a promise of ongoing care.
And then there’s joy. Not the kind that pretends pain doesn’t exist, but the kind that comes from love that shows up, even in hard times. After being anointed, the restless sheep settle down. They graze contentedly, their spirits lighter because someone cared enough to step in. The journey isn’t suddenly easy, but now it’s marked by little moments of relief, laughter, and quiet celebration. The anointing is a gentle reminder: joy is possible, even when life is tough.
So, if you’re longing for healing or a sense of belonging, picture the shepherd’s anointing as a quiet invitation. There’s space for every wound, every irritation, every longing. The shepherd’s care is personal, attentive, and it never runs out. This journey isn’t about escaping pain—it’s about discovering the real joy that comes from being seen, known, and loved.
